prompt: After `UPDATE orders_copy SET status = 'shipped' WHERE id = 7` commits, where is the version of row 7 that said `paid`?
hint: Look at what `heap_page_items` showed for page 0.

choices.text: Overwritten in place by the new value, which is why the ctid stays (0,7)
choices.why: The ctid changed to (8333,41). PostgreSQL never overwrites a row version in place.

choices.text: Copied to the write-ahead log and removed from the table at commit
choices.why: Commit removes nothing from the table. The old version is still on page 0 after it.

choices.text: Still on its page, with xmax set
choices.why: Right. The old version stays where it was until VACUUM frees its space; xmax names the transaction that replaced it.

choices.text: Moved to the free space map, which keeps old versions for readers
choices.why: The free space map records free room per page. It holds no row versions at all.

prompt: A transaction updates one row and then runs `ROLLBACK`. What does it leave in the table?
hint: The update wrote something before it was undone.

choices.text: Nothing: a rollback restores the page exactly
choices.why: The rollback does not erase what was written; n_dead_tup went up by one for it.

choices.text: Two dead versions, the old one and the new one
choices.why: The old version is still the live one after a rollback. Only the new version is dead.

choices.text: One dead version: the new one it wrote
choices.why: Right. The old version stays live, and the version the aborted transaction wrote is the one nobody will ever see.

choices.text: A lock on the row until the next VACUUM
choices.why: Row locks end with the transaction. VACUUM has nothing to do with them.

prompt: The hidden column that names the transaction which wrote a row version is ___.
hint: Its partner, xmax, names the one that replaced it.

prompt: `orders_copy` was 68 MB before and after `VACUUM` cleared 50,000 dead versions. Why did it not shrink?
hint: Where did the freed space go?

choices.text: The dead versions were still visible
choices.why: Nothing held a snapshot then. The dead versions were removed; the space simply stayed in the file.

choices.text: The freed space is free inside the file, for the next rows
choices.why: Right. A plain VACUUM records the room in the free space map; only empty pages at the end of the file are ever cut off.

choices.text: VACUUM shrinks files only after a checkpoint
choices.why: Checkpoints write dirty pages out. They do not change a table's size.

choices.text: pg_relation_size reports the size from the last ANALYZE
choices.why: It reads the files' real size. relpages is the estimate ANALYZE keeps, not this.

prompt: Match each structure to what VACUUM records in it.
hint: One per page about room, two bits per page about visibility, one number per table.

pairs.right: How much room each page has for new rows
Which pages hold only rows every transaction can see, and which are frozen
The oldest transaction id that may still be unfrozen in the table

right_distractors: The planner's estimate of the rows in the table

prompt: An index-only scan on the copy still visits the table for many rows right after a big UPDATE, and stops doing so after a VACUUM. What changed?
hint: What can the scan trust without reading the page?

choices.text: The pages are all-visible again
choices.why: Right. The UPDATE took those pages out of the visibility map, and VACUUM put them back, so the scan can trust the index for them.

choices.text: The index was rebuilt
choices.why: VACUUM removes dead index entries; it does not rebuild the index.

choices.text: The planner's statistics were refreshed by the VACUUM, which is what an index-only scan reads
choices.why: Statistics are ANALYZE's job, and a scan reads the visibility map, not pg_stats, to decide whether to visit a page.

choices.text: The rows were frozen
choices.why: Freezing sets the second bit. The scan needs only the all-visible one, which a plain VACUUM set on all 8,751 pages.

prompt: With the default settings, after how many dead versions does autovacuum vacuum a table whose reltuples is 1,000,000?
hint: 50 plus a fifth.

prompt: After 150,000 rows of the copy were updated, a minute later `last_autoanalyze` had a time and `last_autovacuum` was empty. Why?
hint: Two lines, two scale factors.

choices.text: Autovacuum analyses first and vacuums on its following visit
choices.why: Both are decided on the same visit. The vacuum was not due at all, as the 250,000 case showed.

choices.text: 150,000 is past the analyse line and short of the vacuum line
choices.why: Right: 100,050 for analysing, 200,050 for vacuuming.

choices.text: The worker was cancelled by the UPDATE's lock
choices.why: The UPDATE had finished; nothing was holding a lock on the copy.

choices.text: A table needs its first manual VACUUM before autovacuum will touch it
choices.why: Autovacuum vacuumed orders and customers after the load with nobody typing VACUUM.

prompt: Nobody had updated or deleted a row of `orders` when autovacuum vacuumed it, a minute after the load. Which trigger fired?
hint: A million rows arrived.

choices.text: The wraparound limit
choices.why: The ages were a few dozen transactions, nowhere near 200 million.

choices.text: The insert threshold: rows inserted since the last vacuum
choices.why: Right. 1,000 plus a fifth of the table, and a million inserted rows were far past it.

choices.text: The dead-version threshold, counting the load's rows as dead
choices.why: Inserted rows are live; n_dead_tup stayed at 0.

choices.text: A timer that vacuums every table once a minute
choices.why: The launcher wakes every minute, but it vacuums only tables past a line. orders was not vacuumed again on later rounds.

prompt: A table holds 500 million rows and receives 20 million updates a day. With the default settings, roughly how often is it vacuumed?
hint: Work out a fifth of the table, then divide.

choices.text: Every minute, on each launcher round
choices.why: The launcher looks every minute; it vacuums only past the line, which here is 100 million dead versions.

choices.text: Never, because a table that large is skipped
choices.why: There is no size limit; the line simply rises with the table.

choices.text: Once a day, since 20 million is past the 200,050-row line
choices.why: 200,050 is the line for a table of a million rows. The line scales with reltuples.

choices.text: About every five days
choices.why: Right: 50 + 0.2 x 500 million is about 100 million, which takes five days at 20 million a day. Each pass then clears 100 million versions, which is why such a table gets a scale factor of its own.

prompt: `VACUUM VERBOSE` reports `100000 are dead but not yet removable`. What is the first thing to look for?
hint: Removable depends on who could still see them.

choices.text: A faster disk for autovacuum
choices.why: VACUUM read the pages fine and quickly; speed was not what stopped it.

choices.text: More autovacuum workers
choices.why: More workers would read the same pages and get the same answer.

choices.text: A higher maintenance_work_mem
choices.why: Memory changes how many dead entries fit per pass, not whether they may be removed.

choices.text: A session holding an old snapshot
choices.why: Right. The removable cutoff matched the backend_xmin of the session idle in transaction.

prompt: The idle session had read only `orders_copy`. Would its open snapshot also stop VACUUM removing dead versions from `customers`?
hint: A snapshot is of the database, not of a table.

choices.text: No: a snapshot only protects the tables it has read
choices.why: The snapshot could read any table next. The horizon applies to every table of the database.

choices.text: Yes, and it would also block every INSERT into customers until it ends
choices.why: A snapshot blocks no writes. It only keeps old versions from being removed.

choices.text: No, because customers belongs to another schema
choices.why: Both tables are in public, and schemas have nothing to do with the horizon.

choices.text: Yes, for anything that died after it began
choices.why: Right. The session could still read customers, so everything that died after its snapshot stays, in every table of the database.

prompt: Put the falling-behind demonstration in the order it happened.
hint: The snapshot has to exist before the update for it to matter.
items: Terminal 1 opens a REPEATABLE READ transaction and reads the copy
VACUUM reports them dead but not yet removable
trap: Committing before the second VACUUM is the whole fix; nothing else changed between the two runs.

prompt: VACUUM keeps saying `not yet removable`, and `pg_stat_activity` shows no session older than a few seconds. Where do you look next?
hint: Two things hold the horizon without being sessions.

choices.text: pg_stat_user_tables, to see whether last_autovacuum is recent
choices.why: That shows autovacuum is visiting. The question is what stops it removing anything.

choices.text: The table's reloptions, in case autovacuum is turned off for it
choices.why: A manual VACUUM is reporting the problem, so autovacuum's switch is not the cause.

choices.text: pg_prepared_xacts and pg_replication_slots
choices.why: Right. A forgotten prepared transaction or a slot whose consumer stopped holds the line, and neither appears as a session.

choices.text: pg_settings, for autovacuum_naptime
choices.why: The naptime decides how often autovacuum looks, not what it may remove.

prompt: What would happen to an unfrozen row once its xmin was more than about two billion transactions old?
hint: The numbers are compared on a circle.

choices.text: It would seem to be in the future and vanish from queries
choices.why: Right. That is why freezing exists, and why the server refuses new transaction ids before it can happen.

choices.text: It would be deleted by the next VACUUM
choices.why: VACUUM freezes old rows; it deletes only dead versions.

choices.text: The server would renumber it with a new 64-bit id
choices.why: Row versions carry 32-bit ids, and nothing renumbers them.

choices.text: Nothing: age only matters for statistics
choices.why: The age decides visibility. That is the whole danger.

prompt: On the scratch cluster pushed past the limit, which of these still worked?
hint: What needs a new transaction id?

choices.text: CREATE TABLE t (i int)
choices.why: Creating a table writes to the catalogue and needs a transaction id, so it was refused.

choices.text: SELECT txid_current()
choices.why: txid_current assigns an id if the transaction has none, so it is refused too.

choices.text: An INSERT into an existing table
choices.why: Any write needs a transaction id.

choices.text: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class
choices.why: Right. A read needs no new transaction id, and it answered 413.

prompt: After `vacuumdb --all --freeze`, the scratch cluster still refused writes. Why?
hint: Look at datallowconn.

choices.text: The failsafe had skipped the freezing
choices.why: The failsafe skips index cleanup and throttling, never the freezing; postgres and template1 came back to age 0.

choices.text: The server has to restart before the new ages count
choices.why: Writes worked again with no restart, once template0 was frozen.

choices.text: template0 accepts no connections, so vacuumdb skipped it
choices.why: Right. Autovacuum can reach template0, and within about a minute it had frozen it too.

choices.text: vacuumdb must run in single-user mode to clear the limit
choices.why: It ran with the server up and froze both databases it could reach. Single-user mode was not needed.

prompt: A monitoring graph shows `age(datfrozenxid)` for one database rising steadily past 400 million, while autovacuum_freeze_max_age is 200 million. What does it mean?
hint: Past 200 million an aggressive autovacuum should already have brought it down.

choices.text: Normal growth; act only when the server starts warning
choices.why: The warnings start 40 million before the stop. Waiting for them on a large table leaves no time for a freeze that takes hours.

choices.text: autovacuum is turned off, and turning it on solves it
choices.why: The aggressive autovacuum runs even with autovacuum off, so this alone cannot explain an age that keeps climbing.

choices.text: Autovacuum cannot finish freezing: find what holds the horizon or blocks it
choices.why: Right. Treat it as an incident: an old snapshot, a prepared transaction or a slot is the usual reason.

choices.text: The setting is too low and should be raised to 2 billion
choices.why: Raising the line only moves the alarm closer to the stop. The age climbing past it is the symptom to explain.

prompt: On PostgreSQL 16 with default settings, which autovacuum runs reach the server log?
hint: SHOW log_autovacuum_min_duration.

choices.text: Every one
choices.why: That is a setting of 0, which the lesson put on one table.

choices.text: Those that take ten minutes or more
choices.why: Right. The default is 10min.

choices.text: Only those that remove nothing
choices.why: The setting is about duration, not about what the run achieved.

choices.text: None, unless logging_collector is on
choices.why: Ubuntu's server logs to its file without the collector; the autovacuum line arrived there.

prompt: After `ALTER TABLE orders_copy SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01)`, after how many dead versions is the copy vacuumed?
hint: The threshold stays at 50.

choices.text: 200,050, because a table option does not override the server default
choices.why: A table's own option wins over the server's for that table; the autovacuum after 20,000 updates shows it.
That would be a scale factor of 0.001.
That is the default analyse line, with a scale factor of 0.1.

prompt: A colleague proposes `ALTER TABLE events SET (autovacuum_enabled = false)` because autovacuum on `events` slows the night's batch. What does that lead to?
hint: Which autovacuum still runs?

choices.text: No vacuum of events ever again
choices.why: The aggressive autovacuum against wraparound still comes, whatever this option says.

choices.text: Dead versions pile up until a later, larger, aggressive vacuum
choices.why: Right. Lower the cost of each visit or move it instead; turning the ordinary visits off leaves only the big one.

choices.text: A faster batch and no other effect, since VACUUM can be run by hand later
choices.why: Only if somebody remembers, every time. Meanwhile the table bloats and its age climbs.

choices.text: An error, since autovacuum cannot be set per table
choices.why: Per-table settings are exactly how autovacuum is tuned; the lesson set two of them.

prompt: A table of 2 million rows keeps growing although `last_autovacuum` is updated every few minutes and `n_dead_tup` stays near 3 million. Which explanation fits all of it?
hint: Autovacuum is visiting. What does each visit achieve?

choices.text: The scale factor is too high for the table
choices.why: Then autovacuum would not be visiting every few minutes; it would be waiting for the line.

choices.text: Autovacuum is throttled by its cost delay and never reaches the end of the table, so more workers are needed
choices.why: A throttled run would not finish and update last_autovacuum every few minutes. And more workers would read the same pages.

choices.text: Something holds an old snapshot
choices.why: Right. Frequent visits that leave the dead count high are the signature of a held horizon.

choices.text: The statistics are stale, so n_dead_tup is wrong
choices.why: n_dead_tup is a counter the server keeps, not an ANALYZE estimate, and the file growing agrees with it.

prompt: At 02:00 a report opens a REPEATABLE READ transaction and runs for three hours. Meanwhile the application updates 5 million rows of `orders`. What does autovacuum achieve on `orders` between 02:00 and 05:00?
hint: Which versions died after 02:00?

choices.text: It removes the dead versions as usual, since the report only reads
choices.why: Reading is exactly what needs the old versions; a read-only snapshot holds the horizon too.

choices.text: It cancels the report to clear the table
choices.why: Autovacuum cancels nobody's query; it yields, and the dead versions wait.

choices.text: It is blocked by the report's lock and cannot start
choices.why: A SELECT's lock does not conflict with VACUUM's. Autovacuum runs; it just cannot remove those versions.

choices.text: Nothing on versions that died after 02:00; they go once the report ends
choices.why: Right. The report could still read them, so they stay until its snapshot is gone.

prompt: Match each symptom to what it points at.
hint: Each line is from this lesson's captures.

pairs.left: `dead but not yet removable` stays high run after run
pairs.right: A held snapshot, slot or prepared transaction

pairs.left: `last_autovacuum` empty on a big, busy table
pairs.right: A line too high for the table's size

pairs.left: `must be vacuumed within N transactions` in the log
pairs.right: Transaction id age close to wraparound
Few pages with dead entries, indexes left for later

prompt: You set `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01` on a 300-million-row table. Autovacuum now runs every hour, finishes, and `n_dead_tup` returns to near 0 each time, but the file keeps its size. What should you conclude?
hint: What does a plain VACUUM do with freed space?

choices.text: The setting did not take effect
choices.why: Hourly runs that clear the dead count are the setting working.

choices.text: A snapshot is held, so nothing is removed
choices.why: Then n_dead_tup would stay high. It returns to near 0.

choices.text: The table needs VACUUM (FREEZE) every hour as well, to release its pages to the free space map
choices.why: Freezing is about transaction id age. A plain VACUUM already records freed room in the free space map.

choices.text: It is working: space is reused inside the file
choices.why: Right. A steady size is the goal; giving space back to the operating system is lesson 15's subject.
